questions.q: According to well-documented real-world patterns, which of these is the MOST common way an AWS access key actually ends up leaked?
options: A zero-day exploit against the AWS control plane itself
It is committed to a public GitHub repository and picked up by automated secret-scanning tools within minutes
AWS support staff accidentally email it to the wrong customer
It is brute-forced directly against the AWS API
questions.explain: Secrets committed to public repos are routinely found by automated scanners (the same category as TruffleHog/GitGuardian) almost immediately after the push — this is one of the most common real leak paths, not a sophisticated exploit.

questions.q: What is the significance of IMDSv2's session-token requirement on EC2?
options: It closes the SSRF-to-credential-theft path that let an attacker read an instance's role credentials via IMDSv1
It encrypts all S3 bucket contents automatically
It replaces IAM roles entirely with a new permission model
It is only relevant to Azure, not AWS
questions.explain: IMDSv1 allowed a server-side request forgery vulnerability to reach the instance metadata endpoint and pull temporary credentials with no extra step; IMDSv2 requires a session token first, closing that path.

questions.q: Why do attackers typically run read-only calls like `aws sts get-caller-identity` and `iam list-attached-user-policies` as their FIRST move after obtaining a leaked key?
options: These calls are required by AWS before any other API call will succeed
To immediately trigger GuardDuty so they know what's being monitored
To enumerate what the credential can actually do, quietly, before attempting anything that could fail or get noticed
Because AWS requires a 24-hour waiting period before destructive calls are allowed
questions.explain: Enumeration calls are read-only and look like normal automation, letting an attacker map out what a stolen credential can access before risking a louder action.

questions.q: In the enumerate → escalate → persist → act sequence, what is the main purpose of the persistence step?
options: To make the attack more visible so the victim notices faster
To automatically delete CloudTrail logs
To restore the account to its original state before leaving
To create an independent credential (a second access key, a new IAM user, a new app registration secret) so the attacker keeps access even if the originally leaked credential is rotated
questions.explain: Persistence is about survivability: by creating a second, independent credential before doing anything damaging, the attacker ensures that rotating the original leaked key doesn't end their access.

questions.q: Why is it a mistake for a defender to rely only on detecting the final 'actual abuse' stage (e.g. a cost spike from cryptomining)?
options: Because by that stage the attacker has typically already enumerated the environment and established independent persistence, so simply rotating the original key does not remove their access
Because cost spikes are always false positives
Because AWS does not generate billing alerts
Because cryptomining never actually costs the victim money
questions.explain: Catching only the final, damaging stage means missing the enumeration and persistence steps that already happened — at that point, just rotating the leaked credential leaves any independently created backdoor credential untouched.
